content:
Marissa Cole: Need quick alignment on customer-visible wording for model updates in the autogenerated release notes. We’ve got disagreements on: (1) how we talk about quality/perf changes, (2) what counts as “breaking”, (3) who approves the copy before a promotion ships. Can we settle a v1 policy today?

Paula Mendes: +1. Rollouts/A-B is going to be messy if release notes say “improves quality” and then a customer sees regressions on their prompts. We need language that’s accurate + doesn’t overpromise.

Wei Chen: From docs POV, we can standardize phrasing, but we need a strict rubric for when the generator is allowed to emit “improved” vs “changed”. Also: where does “breaking” land? The current style guide draft has “breaking = requires customer action”, but model behavior is a gray area.

Connor O'Brien: Release Eng concern: if “breaking” is subjective we’ll have bikeshedding in every PR. Ideally it’s computed from metadata fields (compat constraints, tokenizer change, request/response schema change, deprecation, etc.), not a free-text debate.

Dylan Brooks: The generator can map categories, but some of this is editorial. Example: perf: we can show “median latency -8% in Redwood benchmark A” but that may not match every workload. Same for quality.

Jonas Weber: For quality: we should avoid “improved” unless we have statistically significant deltas on a stable eval suite AND we can name the suite. Even then, recommend “Improved on Redwood internal evals (see details)” rather than blanket.

Sana Farid: Agree. Also we need to prevent p-hacking vibes. If we include numbers, we need baselines, confidence intervals, and “may vary by workload.” But for v1 release notes, I’d rather we keep it qualitative and conservative.

Marissa Cole: OK, so proposal:
1) Customer-visible “Quality” section can say either:
- “No expected change in output behavior” (only if eval deltas are within noise + no prompt/template changes)
- “Output behavior changes” (if deltas exist or we changed decoding defaults / safety policies)
- “Improved on Redwood eval suite(s)” (only if Jonas/Sana sign off + required evidence attached)
2) Perf: “Performance characteristics updated” vs “Faster” only if we can reference a benchmark profile + scope.
Thoughts?

Dev Patel: Jumping in from support angle: what customers ask is “did you change the model on me” and “can I roll back.” They don’t care about our p-values. They DO care if their JSON schema started failing or tool calling changed. That’s breaking to them.

Naomi Feldman: Security/compliance angle: release notes must not mention internal incident links, infra vendors, GPU types, specific capacity events, or customer names. Also keep “security” category wording tight (e.g., “security hardening” without describing the exploit).

Jada Williams: Technically, we can detect some breaking cases:
- tokenizer version bump
- chat template change
- function/tool calling schema change
- default parameter changes (temperature/top_p/max_tokens) when customer didn’t set them
But “behavioral drift” is hard.

Paula Mendes: I want “breaking” to include “default changes.” Lots of customers rely on defaults, even if they shouldn’t. If we change default `max_output_tokens` or tool calling strictness, it breaks.

Connor O'Brien: If we broaden “breaking” to “anything might change outputs,” every model update becomes breaking. That will cause alert fatigue.

Wei Chen: Maybe separate:
- “Breaking (API/contract)” = request/response format, endpoints, auth, SDK changes
- “Behavioral breaking” = format/structure changes that could break parsing (JSON mode strictness, tool call args formatting, stop sequences)
And “Quality changes” stays non-breaking unless it affects structured output.

Jonas Weber: +1 to splitting. “Quality” deltas are not “breaking” unless the structured format guarantee is impacted.

Dylan Brooks: This maps well to taxonomy: breaking / behavior / perf / bugfix / deprecation / security.
We should define “Breaking: customer action required to maintain same integration behavior” and list concrete triggers.

Marissa Cole: Concrete triggers list draft (customer-visible breaking):
- Request/response schema change (incl. tool calling payloads)
- Structured output constraints changed (JSON schema, regex format) in a way that can reject previously-valid outputs
- Tokenizer change affecting token counts (could impact max_tokens and cost)
- Removal or rename of model/variant IDs
- Deprecation reaching end-of-life
Non-breaking but notable:
- Default decoding changes (call out under “Behavior changes”)
- Safety policy updates that may refuse more/less content (call out under “Safety/Policy”)
Perf/quality only called out with caveats.

Paula Mendes: I like that, but I’d put “default decoding changes” into “Potentially breaking for some integrations” because it can break deterministic tests.

Connor O'Brien: Could be “Behavior changes (may affect outputs)” with a severity flag (low/med/high). Not labeled “breaking” unless it impacts contract.

Sana Farid: Severity rubric could be tied to evidence:
- low: no significant eval delta, small perf change, doc tweaks
- med: measurable delta on at least 1 suite, new quant profile, batching change, default parameter change
- high: tokenizer/chat template/tool formatting/safety policy update
But we should be careful: “high” implies risk; might scare customers if overused.

Wei Chen: We can phrase severity as “Risk” and use plain language:
- “Low risk: no expected customer action”
- “Medium risk: may affect outputs; consider canary”
- “High risk: may affect output formatting or refusals; recommend pinning/rollback plan”
This aligns with rollouts.

Dev Patel: Support will love “recommend pinning/rollback plan” as a standard line. Also include “how to pin” link.

Naomi Feldman: Redaction reminder: internal-only rationale sometimes includes “customer escalated” or “incident follow-up.” That must not leak. The generator should pull only `public_summary` + `public_impact` fields.

Jada Williams: On workflow: who approves “public_summary”? Right now model registry PRs are mostly Eng.

Connor O'Brien: I propose:
- If release note category includes Breaking/Security/Deprecation OR risk=High => requires approval from Product (Marissa/Paula) + Docs (Wei or Elliot) before promotion.
- Otherwise, Eng lead approval is enough.
We can enforce via CI check: missing approvals blocks merge/promotion.

Elliot Price: (joining) Docs can commit to SLA if it’s limited to those categories. But we need a single place to review the rendered preview, not raw JSON. The preview artifact in CI is perfect.

Marissa Cole: Agree. For v1, approval matrix:
- Breaking / Deprecation: Product + Docs required
- Security: Security reviewer + Product required (docs optional but recommended)
- Quality claims with “Improved”: Jonas/Sana sign-off + Product + Docs
- Everything else: Eng + optional Docs
Does that feel workable?

Dylan Brooks: Works for me. Implementation detail: the generator should refuse “Improved” unless `quality_evidence_ids` present and `quality_claim_level=measured` (or similar). Otherwise it downgrades to “Updated” language.

Jonas Weber: +1. Also “Improved” should name the eval suite class, not the metric. e.g., “Improved on Redwood instruction-following evals” not “+2.1%” unless we’re ready to publish methodology.

Sana Farid: And we should add: “Results may vary by prompt and domain; recommend A/B test” as a standard disclaimer when any quality section is present.

Wei Chen: If we add disclaimers everywhere, release notes become unreadable. Maybe disclaimers only on Medium/High risk behavior/quality changes.

Paula Mendes: +1. Keep it scannable.

Marissa Cole: OK, wording guidance:
- Perf:
  - Allowed: “Reduced latency on Redwood benchmark profiles for typical context lengths (may vary).”
  - Not allowed: “2x faster” unless it’s an externally published benchmark.
- Quality:
  - Default: “No expected change” / “Output behavior changes (see details)”
  - “Improved” only with evidence + sign-off.
- Breaking:
  - Must include “What you may need to change” + link to docs.
- Behavior changes:
  - Include risk level and rollback guidance.
Everyone ok?

Connor O'Brien: Works. I’ll translate into a checklist for release train + required PR labels.

Elliot Price: Please include examples of “good vs bad” phrasing. Otherwise reviewers will keep rewriting.

Dev Patel: + include one line that tells support what to ask customers for: model id, version, deployment mode, region, rollout policy.

Naomi Feldman: Add to checklist: ensure no internal ticket IDs, customer names, or incident references in public fields.

Jada Williams: Action items:
- Marissa/Paula: finalize breaking triggers + risk rubric copy
- Connor: approval matrix + CI gate proposal
- Wei/Elliot: style guide snippets + examples
- Jonas/Sana: define what evidence is sufficient for “Improved” claim
I’ll open a follow-up doc.

Marissa Cole: Great. Let’s treat this as v1 and iterate after beta feedback. I’ll post the agreed language in the PRD + ping everyone.

Connor O'Brien: :thumbsup: I’ll also propose defaulting `risk=medium` when metadata indicates template/tokenizer/default changes and requiring an explicit override to lower.

Sana Farid: :+1: but make overrides auditable.

Naomi Feldman: and overrides should show up in audit logs (internal) even if not public.

Marissa Cole: Noted. Closing the loop here — thanks all.
